newsitem.title: DUBAI: Qatar gets second wind as oil and gas producer.
newsitem.headline: Qatar gets second wind as oil and gas producer.

text.p: Cash-strapped Qatar is getting a second wind as an oil producer just months before the Gulf Arab state enters the ring as a major gas exporter, oil industry sources in Qatar said on Wednesday.

Though overshadowed in reserves in neighbouring Saudi Arabia, oil output in Qatar is forecast to rise by more than 40 percent in the next four years to 700,000 barrels per day (bpd) as international energy firms develop new fields.
An early boost to the Doha exchequer -- which relies on oil for more than 65 percent of its income -- will be first production from the offshore Al-Rayyan field next month.

"The best estimate is production at Al-Rayyan will start in early October...the first cargo will be ready in the first week of November," said Paul Fronterhouse, vice president of Atlantic Richfield Co (ARCO) in Qatar, the field operator.
Al-Rayyan output will be gradually increased to a full rate of 35,000 barrels per day (bpd) after start-up, adding to OPEC member Qatar's current estimated total output of 480,000 bpd.

Qatar's $6 billion Qatargas LNG project will start to pay off its massive investment in December when the first gas cargo is loaded for sale to Japan. Exports of light oil condensate from the gas field run by Qatargas is expected this month.
From then on Doha can reap the fruits of the world's largest single reservoir of gas -- the North Field -- with recoverable reserves exceeding 380 trillion cubic feet.
Foreign firms with production-sharing agreements with the state-owned Qatar General Petroleum Corp (QGPC) are also planning to boost oil flows from Qatar's offshore deposits.

Denmark's Maersk Oil has requested engineering firms to bid for work to expand facilities at its 45,000 bpd Al-Shaheen field to 150,000 bpd before the end of this decade, contractors based in the Gulf region said.

French firm Elf Aquitaine is expected to bring its Al-Khaleej field onstream early next year at 25,000 bpd before rising to 45,000 bpd while Canadian Occidental Petroleum is studying ways of boosting recovery rates at its 70,000 bpd Idd Al Shargi concession.
These increases are expected to push Qatar oil output above its current OPEC quota of 378,000 bpd.

A recent study by the International Monetary Fund estimates that Doha's oil revenue will rise to $3.3 billion in 2001 from $2.1 billion in 1995 while revenue from the sale of liquefied natural gas (LNG) from its three planned LNG projects will reach $1.9 billion in 2001.
Qatar's Marine export grade was trading at around $22.30 a barrel fob Qatar on Wednesday.

The extra revenues will come as a relief to Doha which is burdened with a external debt of some $6 billion, deficits of more than 10 percent of GDP and a court battle against its former and now exiled emir to recover state oil revenue.
"The money squeeze that has blighted the local economy for much of the nineties should ease," one Western industry executive based in the country said.
Infrastructural projects outside the energy sector have been delayed as Doha devoted available funds to meet financing commitments to develop the multi-billion gas projects.
